## 1. Introduction

Tissue perfusion plays a crucial role in a range of physiological and pathological processes, making its monitoring essential in clinical practice [1]. Accurate, real-time assessment is important in areas such as surgery, critical care, and the diagnosis of vascular disease [2]. Continuous and reliable monitoring is particularly critical during complex reconstructive procedures, including vascularized composite allotransplantation and free flap transfer, where early detection of vascular compromise can determine graft survival [3].

Traditional approaches to assessing tissue perfusion often rely on invasive techniques, which can introduce risks and complications [4], or require substantial training and attention from care providers. Consequently, non-invasive, imaging-based methods have received increasing attention.

Multi-modal imaging combines information from different sensor modalities, such as Laser Speckle Contrast Imaging (LSCI), thermal imaging, and RGB cameras, to provide a more comprehensive assessment of tissue perfusion [5]. Each modality offers distinct information: near-IR LSCI captures blood-flow dynamics, far-IR thermal imaging detects temperature variations, and RGB imaging provides structural detail [6] as well as discoloration associated with occlusion. Because each modality also has inherent limitations, fusion-based approaches can provide a more complete view of tissue perfusion [7].

Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have achieved substantial success in medical imaging applications, including segmentation, classification, and anomaly detection [8]. Fusion methods such as early fusion, channel-based fusion using 2, 4, or 5 channels, and late fusion seek to combine multi-modal data to improve model robustness and accuracy [9]. Despite recent progress, challenges remain in accurately aligning different modalities, addressing cross-modal variation, and optimizing fusion strategies for clinical use [10]. In addition, literature from the past five years indicates a growing interest in advanced deep learning architectures, including spatial–temporal fusion frameworks, for addressing challenges in multi-modal medical imaging [11,12]. Previous studies have shown that even relatively low-resolution thermal sensors can effectively detect perforators [13,14,15,16,17,18]. Several non-invasive and invasive technologies have been developed to improve the accuracy of clinical examinations [19], but none has been universally adopted.

Although the different sensing modalities are intended to capture distinct physiological responses to occlusion, prior work did not ensure calibration between the modal images. Differences in camera resolution and viewing angle can therefore produce misalignment and suboptimal performance. As a result, the CNN must learn more complex relationships at higher layers, using larger receptive fields to account for offsets between camera views. With proper alignment, the network can learn multi-spectral features at the lowest level, which are expected to improve contextual representation and classification performance.

In this study, we evaluated the effectiveness of different fusion techniques for tissue perfusion analysis using ResNet50 and ResNet101 models. The study uses the Tourniquet Tissue Perfusion Dataset (TTPD), which is divided into two experiments: Pass2, the calibrated dataset, and Unseen, the generalization dataset. We also introduced homography-based calibration to improve the spatial alignment of multi-modal images and enhance fusion performance.

The experimental results provide insight into how fusion strategies and calibration methods affect deep learning-based perfusion analysis. They highlight the value of image alignment and the need for larger tissue perfusion datasets.

### 3. Fusion and Classification

#### 3.1. Classifiers

In this study, we used ResNet50 and ResNet101 because of their established effectiveness in feature extraction and deep representation learning for medical image analysis. ResNet50 has a 50-layer architecture and offers a balance between computational efficiency and performance. This makes it suitable for processing the complex patterns found in angiographic images while keeping training times feasible [22]. ResNet101, by contrast, is a deeper 101-layer variant that can capture more intricate hierarchical features, which may help distinguish subtle differences in vascular structures [23].

During the preliminary experiments, lightweight CNN architectures, including SqueezeNet and GoogleNet, were also evaluated. However, they produced lower classification accuracy on this complex multi-modal dataset. Vision transformers (ViTs) and medical transformer encoders provide substantial capacity, but they are notoriously data-hungry and highly susceptible to severe overfitting on constrained datasets because they lack inductive biases. For this reason, ResNet50 and ResNet101 were deliberately selected as the primary backbone networks, providing a robust, well-understood, and optimal baseline that naturally resists overfitting on limited medical data.

Using these standardized CNN backbones also allows the study to isolate and quantify the specific performance gains associated with Homography-based spatial calibration and the multi-modal fusion strategies, while reducing the confounding effects of architectural complexity. The selected models support a comparative assessment of how network depth affects detection performance while maintaining robust feature extraction capabilities.

#### 3.2. Fusion

The multi-modal nature of the TTPD enables the detection of different cues: blackening or discoloration in RGB images, temperature drops in thermal images, and surface vessels in laser images. Feature fusion (Figure 3) provides a way to combine these sensors within a single network and exploit their complementary information. Highly complex, state-of-the-art fusion algorithms could potentially obscure the fundamental improvements obtained purely from spatial alignment. Therefore, basic and well-understood early and late fusion methods were used so that the observed performance increases could be attributed directly to Homography calibration.

Several feature fusion methods, including early and late fusion approaches proposed in the literature [24,25], have been applied to perfusion analysis [20]. Early fusion, shown on the left-hand side of Figure 3, combines the image modalities as separate channels before modeling with a CNN network. Late fusion, shown on the right-hand side of Figure 3, processes each modality separately using an optimized modeling network and then combines the individual results to produce the final output [20].

Early fusion was implemented in two ways: early blend and 2-4-5 channel fusion. Early blend is intended for direct use with the ResNet architectures without modification. To produce a standardized three-channel input, denoted as \(I_{EB}\), an arithmetic mean is calculated across the \(N\) selected modalities \((I_1, I_2, \ldots, I_N)\):

\[
I_{EB}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} I_i
\tag{1}
\]

Here, \(N\) denotes the number of modalities being fused, such as \(N=2\) for thermal and RGB or \(N=3\) for LSCI, thermal, and RGB. This generalized formulation assigns equal weighting to all input modalities, ensuring that each sensor contributes proportionally to the fused feature map without bias.

In early 2-4-5 channel fusion, the image modalities are combined by stacking channels. Laser and thermal images are treated as single grayscale channels, whereas RGB images are treated as three channels. The final fusion image, \(I_{245}\), is generated through channel-wise concatenation, denoted by \(\operatorname{cat}(\cdot)\):

\[
I_{245}=\operatorname{cat}(\operatorname{cat}(I_1,I_2),I_3)
\tag{2}
\]

To support four- and five-channel inputs in the ResNet architecture, the pre-trained three-channel ImageNet weights of the first convolutional layer were averaged and replicated across the additional input channels. This allowed the network to use the learned feature extractors seamlessly.

This paper presents a novel RSS method for scenarios involving identical modulation types and overlapping parameter ranges. For the digitized PDW data obtained through preprocessing, a one-dimensional neural network, termed U1DADM, is developed based on the concept of semantic segmentation. A mask-assisted strategy is also introduced to improve the network’s ability to perceive and identify overlapping pulses within the same time unit.

For data preprocessing, the proposed digitized PDW representation preserves the complete intra-pulse and inter-pulse feature information while maintaining a unified input length. It also effectively alleviates the non-stationarity and non-convergence problems caused by the continuous temporal growth of TOA data, thereby improving training stability and feature-learning capability.

In terms of network architecture, the ADC module in U1DADM dynamically adjusts the dilation coefficient to match the sparsity characteristics of different pulse data, allowing the network receptive field to be adjusted flexibly. At the same time, a multi-scale feature fusion mechanism strengthens the modeling of long-range correlated features, enabling the network to capture deep semantic relationships in complex pulse streams. The down-sampling modules further expand the receptive field and extract abstract semantic information in a higher-level feature space. The up-sampling modules progressively restore feature resolution and pulse-position information, while skip connections reduce the loss of local details during down-sampling by combining shallow and deep features.

For the masking assistance strategy, pulse-overlap mask information is introduced to support model training because multiple pulses may overlap within the same time unit in digitized PDW data, making them difficult for the network to distinguish accurately. This strategy improves the network’s ability to identify overlapping pulse regions and enhances pulse separation performance in complex scenarios.

Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively fuses multidimensional pulse information with deep semantic features, enabling accurate radar signal sorting under identical modulation types and overlapping parameter ranges. In addition, the method demonstrates strong generalization and robustness under complex conditions, including measurement errors, false pulses, missing pulses, and different pulse stream densities.

This paper proposes an RSS method for scenarios involving identical modulation types and overlapping parameter ranges. For digitized PDW data obtained after preprocessing, it designs a one-dimensional neural network, termed U1DADM, based on semantic segmentation. It also introduces a mask-assisted strategy to improve the network’s ability to perceive and recognize overlapping pulses within the same time unit.

It also improves the non-stationarity and non-convergence issues caused by the continuous temporal growth of TOA data. As a result, network training becomes more stable and feature-learning capability improves.

In U1DADM, the ADC module dynamically adjusts the dilation coefficient to match the sparsity characteristics of different pulse data and adjust the network receptive field accordingly. A multi-scale feature fusion mechanism improves the modeling of long-range correlated features. This enables the network to capture deep semantic relationships within complex pulse streams. The down-sampling modules further enlarge the receptive field and extract abstract semantic information in higher-level feature space. The up-sampling modules progressively restore feature resolution and pulse-position information. Skip connections reduce the loss of local detail during down-sampling by integrating shallow and deep features.

The masking assistance strategy addresses the difficulty of distinguishing multiple pulses that overlap within the same time unit in digitized PDW data. Pulse-overlap mask information is introduced to assist model training. This strategy improves the network’s ability to perceive overlapping pulse regions and enhances pulse separation performance in complex scenarios.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively fuses multidimensional pulse information and extracts deep semantic features. It therefore enables accurate radar signal sorting under identical modulation types and overlapping parameter ranges. The method also exhibits strong generalization and robustness under complex conditions, including measurement errors, false pulses, missing pulses, and different pulse-stream densities.

results.A: 5. ConclusionsThis paper presented an SE-EfficientNetV2-S framework with two-stage semi-supervised training evaluated on a 10-class NWPU-RESISC45 subset. Key conclusions are as follows.The purely supervised SE-EfficientNetV2-S establishes a strong and competitive lightweight baseline. With 20.4 M parameters and 98.71% independent test accuracy, it surpasses the considerably larger ResNet50 (98.50%, 24.1 M parameters) at roughly 85% of its parameter count. This result demonstrates that careful training protocol—specifically, fully unfrozen fine-tuning from ImageNet pre-trained weights without restrictive layer-wise freezing—rather than sheer model size or architectural complexity, is the primary driver of strong performance on fine-grained remote sensing scene classification. The proposed framework thus provides a robust and reproducible supervised baseline for resource-constrained deployment scenarios.SE channel attention shows a seed-sensitive gain that does not reach robust reproducibility at the current dataset scale. On the reported seed, the SE module contributed a +0.21 pp improvement in test accuracy (98.50% → 98.71%) with negligible parameter overhead (~0.2 M additional parameters). However, multi-seed evaluation across three independent initializations shows this advantage reverses on one seed and disappears entirely in the cross-seed mean, with both SE and No-SE configurations converging to 98.71% ± 0.15–0.17%. The SE module’s accuracy benefit under pure supervision should therefore be treated as an initialization-sensitive effect rather than a consistently reproducible architectural advantage at the current 10-class, single-split dataset scale.Semi-supervised pseudo-labeling shows a small, architecture-dependent test-set effect. Across three independent seeds, the No-SE configuration gains a mean + 0.45 pp (±0.36 pp) in test accuracy under semi-supervised fine-tuning (98.71% → 99.17%), consistent in sign across all three seeds but not statistically significant at this sample size (paired t(2) ≈ 2.2, p ≈ 0.16). For the SE-augmented model, the corresponding gain is marginal (+0.08 pp; 98.71% → 98.79%), indicating that the channel gating mechanism moderates the effectiveness of pseudo-label augmentation. Validation accuracy improved substantially for both configurations (→99.43% and 99.57%, respectively), but the larger test gains for the No-SE variant suggest that validation metrics alone should not be treated as the sole indicator of generalization when the unlabeled pool is drawn from the same distribution as the training data.Multi-seed analysis reveals that SE and semi-supervision interact in category-specific ways. Under semi-supervised fine-tuning, the No-SE configuration achieves both a higher mean overall test accuracy (99.17% vs. 98.79%) and lower per-class variance than the SE-augmented model across most categories—most notably in forest (No-SE: ±0.45 pp; SE: ±0.79 pp) and industrial area (No-SE: ±0.33 pp; SE: ±0.71 pp). This suggests that the SE gating mechanism, while beneficial under clean supervised training, amplifies the effect of incorrect pseudo-labels in small-data regimes. Because the P90 relative threshold identifies vehicles traveling markedly faster than their fleet peers under the same road and time conditions, speed-related exceedances are inherently more common than the relatively rare directional events, namely sharp turning and sharp lane changing. This imbalance should be considered when interpreting the per-category performance metrics, since the larger number of speeding samples provides more training instances for that category.

A key methodological contribution of this study is the use of a P90-based relative thresholding strategy for behavior labeling. In contrast to fixed empirical thresholds, this approach derives behavior boundaries from fleet-specific driving distributions and can therefore adapt to real operating conditions. This design is especially relevant to hazardous chemical transportation vehicles, whose regulatory requirements and operating characteristics differ from those of general traffic.

The validity of the proposed labeling strategy is supported by several complementary analyses. First, the derived thresholds are consistent with values reported in previous studies of risky driving behavior. Second, sensitivity analysis using different percentile settings (P85, P90, and P95) shows that model performance remains stable, indicating robustness to the choice of threshold. Third, 120 events identified by the thresholds were cross-checked against onboard video data, and 89% were judged consistent with the observed driving maneuvers, providing additional observational evidence of label reliability.

The comparison with the baseline models further demonstrates the advantages of the proposed framework. Random Forest delivered stable performance, whereas BP neural networks were more sensitive to class imbalance. The ELM-AdaBoost model provided a better balance between accuracy and generalization. In addition, the boosting mechanism reduced the instability associated with randomly initialized ELM models, improving robustness across all behavior categories.

The P90 percentile system should be understood as a surrogate proxy for driving risk rather than as an externally calibrated ground truth. The relative speeding margin is calculated from the same P90 statistics used to define the speeding label, meaning that part of the labeling information is structurally embedded in the feature space. Accordingly, the reported accuracy reflects the model’s ability to reproduce a statistically consistent, fleet-referenced risk criterion, rather than its performance against externally observed crash outcomes. Recent work has likewise discussed the completeness and validation of surrogate-based models in transportation machine learning [29].

In this study, external validation was limited to the onboard-video cross-check, in which 89% of the inspected events were consistent with observable risky maneuvers. Systematic calibration against crash or near-miss records was not possible because no such incident occurred among the labeled events during the monitoring period. Establishing the operational validity of the P90 threshold using independent crash or near-miss data is therefore left for future work. To further assess whether the classifier simply reproduced the embedded threshold information, an ablation study of the relative speeding margin was also conducted (Section Ablation Analysis of the Relative Speeding Margin).

Overall, the proposed framework combines adaptive label construction with efficient ensemble learning, enabling accurate recognition of risky driving behavior from GPS trajectory data. results.A: 5. DiscussionA key methodological consideration in our multi-modal early fusion framework concerns the resolution alignment across the distinct imaging spectrums. While the near-IR (2000 × 2000) and RGB (1200 × 1200) data captured high-frequency structural and surface capillary details, they were downsampled to match the spatial dimensions of the thermal sensor (640 × 480) to construct the joint 640 × 480 × 5 tensor. Although this spatial scaling inevitably reduces fine-grained localized texture resolution, the early fusion strategy demonstrated robust classification capabilities by successfully capturing cross-spectral feature correlations from the initial layers of the deep network. This implies that the macro-level spatial distribution of thermal per-perfusion patterns, when coupled with multi-spectral tissue characteristics, provides highly discriminative representations for classifying tourniquet stages, effectively mitigating the impact of localized resolution loss. Future iterations of this work will explore multi-scale feature pyramid networks to leverage native resolutions simultaneously without encountering architectural misalignment.In this study, spatial registration across the multi-modal sensors was achieved by leveraging a planar Homography calibration matrix. It is important to acknowledge that the hand is a three-dimensional deformable object, and Homography fundamentally assumes a planar geometry, which inevitably introduces minor parallax registration errors at the curved extremities. Furthermore, traditional full 3D stereo calibration relies on checkerboard targets which suffer from rapid heat dissipation, making precise 3D corner detection with thermal sensors highly unreliable. Due to this hardware constraint, and because state-of-the-art (SOTA) 3D medical image registration pipelines incur significant computational overhead prohibitive for real-time monitoring, 2D Homography was implemented. This purposeful trade-off prioritizes low-latency, real-time inference while maintaining robust spatial alignment for the macroscopic regions of interest.Given the substantial parameter footprint associated with deep convolutional architectures like ResNet-101, mitigating the risk of overfitting on a clinically constrained dataset was a critical priority in our experimental design. To safeguard against this, we heavily utilized transfer learning protocols with pre-trained weights, restricting fine-tuning primarily to the newly introduced multi-modal fusion layers. Furthermore, tissue perfusion and blood flow dynamics are inherently non-stationary processes, which poses a challenge for static artificial neural networks (ANNs). Our transition lag analysis (Table 4) effectively mitigated the labeling noise caused by this physiological delay by excluding the ambiguous transition window. Future studies will explore spatiotemporal networks, such as LSTMs or temporal vision transformers, to better model these dynamic, non-stationary transitions.Additionally, while this pilot study primarily reports overall accuracy to validate the technical feasibility of the multi-modal calibration, we acknowledge that accuracy alone may mask class-specific performance. Due to the constrained 10-subject sample size, rigorous paired statistical testing or bootstrap confidence intervals were not conducted. Future large-scale clinical evaluations using our upgraded V2 hardware will encompass comprehensive class-wise metrics (e.g., F1-score, sensitivity, specificity, and precision) and rigorous statistical significance testing to firmly establish the superiority of specific fusion strategies across diverse clinical conditions.

7. Conclusions and Future Work

### 7.1. Conclusions

This work addresses trustworthy environmental-state construction in resource-constrained smart agriculture IoT systems, where sensor observations may be noisy or adversarial. Rather than treating trust as an abstract assumption, we designed and implemented a complete system that combines Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), Byzantine-robust aggregation, and a lightweight permissioned blockchain to support verifiable environmental-state consensus.

The proposed framework is built around three distinct but coordinated trust layers: execution integrity at the edge, data reliability through robust aggregation, and state-level consistency through blockchain commitment. Within this architecture, TEEs provide hardware-assisted protection for sensor-data preprocessing and attestation, ensuring that data entering the system originates from verified execution contexts. A Byzantine-resilient aggregation mechanism then filters corrupted or manipulated readings and constructs a consistent environmental state from distributed observations. Finally, the permissioned blockchain records only validated state commitments, enabling tamper-evident and traceable evolution of the system state.

Unlike traditional blockchain–IoT systems that record raw sensor data directly or depend solely on cryptographic integrity, this framework is designed to preserve the consistency of the derived environmental state under adversarial sensing conditions. Blockchain consequently serves as a coordination and finality layer rather than as a transactional ledger, allowing lightweight consensus appropriate for IoT-scale deployments.

Experimental results from a real greenhouse IoT prototype show that the proposed architecture significantly improves robustness against sensor corruption and adversarial perturbation. Compared with a baseline without Byzantine aggregation, the system maintains stable state estimation and consistent blockchain commitments as sensing interference increases. The results also indicate that TEE-assisted preprocessing strengthens resistance to gateway-level compromise, while its combination with robust aggregation prevents corrupted observations from reaching the consensus layer.

The experiments also reveal that system reliability is preserved through adaptive commitment behavior. When sensing uncertainty exceeds the aggregation tolerance, the system naturally reduces or suspends state commitment, thereby preventing corrupted environmental states from being recorded on-chain. This demonstrates that consensus functions as a safety-preserving mechanism rather than simply as a continuous data-logging process.

### 7.2. Limitations and Future Work

The current prototype was evaluated in a controlled greenhouse environment, which may not fully represent the scale and heterogeneity of large industrial agricultural deployments. Future work will therefore focus on extending the system to large-scale sensor networks with dynamic topologies and heterogeneous device capabilities.

The adversarial model examined in this study primarily addresses data-level manipulation and partial node compromise. More advanced threats, including coordinated multi-node collusion, adaptive adversarial behavior, and cross-layer attack strategies, remain to be investigated.

The current consensus layer also uses a lightweight permissioned design intended for edge environments. Future research may examine hierarchical consensus architectures that combine edge-level state agreement with higher-level regional coordination.

Finally, this work points toward integrating trustworthy sensing, distributed estimation, and blockchain-based coordination into a unified framework for cyber–physical systems beyond agriculture, including environmental monitoring and industrial IoT applications.

5. Blockchain-Driven Trusted Execution

### 5.1. Blockchain Virtual Machine and Computational Model

The proposed architecture is built around a Blockchain Virtual Machine (BVM), which provides an abstract execution layer for deploying smart contracts and performing decentralized computation. The BVM supports general-purpose programmable logic for IoT coordination and data-driven decision-making. In principle, smart contracts deployed on the BVM can implement arbitrary deterministic computations, provided that execution remains within the applicable resource limits.

To ensure that execution remains practical, the system applies bounded execution semantics through resource-control mechanisms such as gas metering or instruction limits. These restrictions prevent non-termination and reduce the risk of denial-of-service behaviors while retaining the expressiveness needed by decentralized applications.

### 5.2. Immutable Ledger and Cryptographic Commitment

The blockchain ledger is represented as an ordered sequence of blocks, \(B=(B_1,B_2,\ldots,B_k)\), with each block defined as (7). Assuming that the underlying hash function \(h(\cdot)\) is collision-resistant and that the signature scheme is existentially unforgeable under chosen-message attacks (EUF-CMA), the ledger provides tamper-evident integrity. Modifying historical data would require recomputing a valid cryptographic chain, which is computationally infeasible under standard cryptographic assumptions.

To support scalable IoT data processing, the system stores data off-chain while maintaining cryptographic commitments on-chain. Each off-chain data object \(D_i^{off}\) is linked to a commitment defined by (6), which is recorded on-chain to bind the external data to the immutable ledger. This arrangement allows large-scale or privacy-sensitive data to remain off-chain while retaining verifiability through hash-based authentication. When data is retrieved for processing or auditing, integrity is verified by recomputing the cryptographic digest and comparing it with the recorded value.

### 5.3. Trusted Execution Environment as Fixed System Assumption

The proposed architecture assumes that selected edge nodes provide a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). This TEE is supplied by the underlying deployment infrastructure, such as ARM TrustZone/OP-TEE-enabled gateways, and serves as a fixed trusted execution substrate.

The TEE is not treated as a tunable or evaluated component in this work. It remains unchanged across all experimental configurations and is excluded from the ablation study. Consequently, the performance differences reported in this paper are attributed not to variations in TEE implementation or availability, but to differences in the consensus-layer and aggregation-layer designs.

Within this assumed trusted environment, off-chain data integrity can be verified securely. When a data object \(D_i^{off}\) is accessed, the enclave computes \(h(D_i^{off})\) and compares it with the on-chain commitment \(h_{on-chain}\):

\[
Verify(D_i^{off},h_{on-chain})=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } h(D_i^{off})=h_{on-chain},\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\tag{9}
\]

This verification is performed within the trusted hardware boundary. In the experimental design, however, it remains a constant system primitive rather than a variable under evaluation.

### 5.4. Logic Decomposition and Ablation Scope

To clarify the attribution of performance improvements, the system is explicitly divided into three conceptual layers:

- **Trusted Execution Layer:** Provides secure execution through the TEE. This layer is fixed, identical across all experimental settings, and excluded from the ablation space.
- **Aggregation Layer:** Defines how multi-source IoT updates are combined, including Vanilla aggregation (no robust filtering), statistical aggregation (mean-based), and Byzantine-resilient aggregation mechanisms.
- **Confirmation Layer:** Applies K-confirmation logic to transaction finality under probabilistic consensus guarantees.

Accordingly, the ablation study considers only variations in the aggregation and confirmation layers while keeping the trusted execution environment constant.

### 5.5. Consensus Robustness and Probabilistic Finality

To quantify security against chain-reorganization attacks, we use a probabilistic model based on the adversarial control fraction \(\alpha\). The probability that an adversary can successfully rewrite a block after \(k\) confirmations is bounded by (10):

\[
P_{rewrite}\leq \left(\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\right)^k,
\qquad \text{for } \alpha<0.5.
\tag{10}
\]

This expression represents the exponential decrease in attack success probability as the confirmation depth increases and provides a formal justification for K-confirmation-based finality.

### 5.6. Workflow Integration

The overall workflow combines blockchain execution, off-chain data commitment, and trusted verification within a unified architecture. IoT devices generate data that is stored off-chain and committed on-chain using cryptographic hashes. Aggregation and consensus mechanisms operate on these committed values to maintain consistency and fault tolerance. When verification is needed, execution is invoked through the TEE under the assumption of a trusted substrate, allowing integrity to be validated without exposing sensitive computation to the untrusted environment.

The Trusted Execution Environment is not a variable in the experimental evaluation. All reported performance differences result from the design of the aggregation and confirmation mechanisms under identical trusted execution conditions. Thus, the ablation results isolate the contribution of the proposed consensus-layer improvements rather than differences in the underlying hardware security infrastructure.

Chen et al. [28] utilized alternating spatial and channel attention in consecutive Transformer blocks, aggregating inter-block features to enhance the extraction of high-frequency details. Rossi et al. [29] upgraded the Swin2SR model by introducing an enhanced sparse-gated hybrid expert layer to replace the Transformer’s internal feed-forward network, thereby enhancing overall performance. Building upon such efficient gating mechanisms, multi-scale gated networks [30] have also been recently developed to achieve an optimal balance between image restoration quality and computational cost. [33] introduced a novel hybrid multi-axis aggregation network to better explore latent feature information.Pixel-level attention provides another effective strategy for spatially non-uniform image super-resolution. The Pixel Attention Network generates three-dimensional attention maps to adaptively recalibrate individual spatial-channel features, enabling different image regions to receive content-dependent responses [34]. Meanwhile, structured doubly stochastic similarity learning constrains an affinity matrix through non-negativity and balanced row- and column-wise normalization, thereby reducing excessively concentrated or one-sided correspondences [35]. In addition to deterministic CNN- and Transformer-based methods, normalizing flows offer a probabilistic alternative for image super-resolution. SRFlow explicitly learns the conditional distribution of plausible high-resolution images given a low-resolution input, addressing the one-to-many nature of the SR problem [36]. This section describes the development of several FPGA-based hardware architectures. CAMC is therefore used as a representative MAC-intensive SDR workload for investigating the scalability of FPGA-based SDR implementations, rather than as a direct implementation of a specific 6G sensing application. A datapath-only hardware architecture using Direct Memory Access (DMA) was also implemented to emulate a data-transfer-only function.

Figure 1 shows the CAMC hardware architecture and its associated peripherals. The full SDR functionality is implemented using peripheral modules including the BRAM Controller, BRAM Generator, DMA, and AXI Interconnect. I/Q data is initially transferred to the CAMC hardware in the FPGA fabric from a High-Performance (HP) port of the Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC through the AXI Interconnect and DMA. The AXI Stream protocol is used to support high transfer speeds. After receiving the data from the DMA, the CAMC module performs the algorithm within the FPGA fabric. The processed data is then stored directly in the FPGA BRAM. All AXI Stream ports are connected to the HP ports to provide high-speed data transmission between the MPSoC and FPGA. All IP cores are connected to the master ports so that they can be properly controlled by the MPSoC.

The HP ports provide the primary interface for high-throughput data transfer between the programmable logic (PL) and DDR memory. Their performance is influenced by both deterministic traffic from PL masters and non-deterministic traffic generated by processor-driven software. Through configurable controls, HP ports enable designers to shape memory access patterns, thereby supporting efficient DDR bandwidth utilisation and high-performance system operation [21].

In this configuration, the I/Q data is transferred from a High-Performance (HP) port of the Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC through the AXI Interconnect to the DMA and then returned. The AXI Interconnect on the right functions as the controller for the DMA modules. This design provides a reference framework for estimating the available FPGA resources and bandwidth when integrating custom SDR hardware accelerators.

The “CAMC and its peripherals” architecture follows the design presented in Figure 1, whereas the “Datapath-only and its peripherals” architecture corresponds to Figure 2. These two hardware implementations provide reference designs for evaluating the scalability of FPGA-based SDR systems and examining the trade-offs among bandwidth, operating frequency, and resource utilisation as the degree of parallelism increases.

## 1. Introduction

Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR) is a fundamental computer vision task that aims to recover high-fidelity details from degraded, low-resolution (LR) observations. In addition to its theoretical importance, SISR has been explored as a preprocessing technique for several domain-specific imaging tasks, including medical imaging [1,2], biometric analysis [3,4], and remote sensing [5,6]. However, the present study focuses exclusively on standard natural-image SR benchmarks and does not directly evaluate these application scenarios. By estimating missing high-frequency information with sophisticated algorithms, SISR offers an effective computational approach for improving image reconstruction quality from low-resolution observations.

Super-resolution (SR) is inherently ill-posed because a single low-resolution image can correspond to a large number of high-resolution images rather than to one unique result. Earlier studies primarily employed interpolation-based [7], reconstruction-based [8], and learning-based [9] approaches to generate super-resolution images. Among these, learning-based methods generally rely on neural networks to reconstruct images with improved quality.

Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based methods have achieved strong performance in single-image super-resolution by learning complex nonlinear mappings through deep convolutional architectures. Kim et al. [10], for example, developed the Very Deep Super-Resolution (VDSR) model, which uses twenty convolutional layers and cascaded small filters within a deep architecture. Tai et al. [11] proposed the Deep Recursive Residual Network (DRRN), combining recursive structures with residual learning to increase network depth while controlling the parameter footprint. Lai et al. [12] subsequently introduced the Deep Laplacian Pyramid Super-Resolution Network (LapSRN), which uses recurrent layers to share parameters across pyramid levels, reducing parameter redundancy and improving reconstruction quality.

Attention mechanisms have also been widely incorporated into SR networks to help models focus on important regions. Zhang et al. [13] developed the Deep Residual Channel Attention Network (RCAN), which combines long skip connections with channel attention to improve reconstruction accuracy. Xu et al. [14] constructed the EASR network using Enhanced Densely Connected Attention Residual Groups. Yu et al. [15] proposed the reference-based R-DHAN, which uses a texture transfer backbone (SRNTT) to recover rich details at ×4 magnification. Qin et al. [16] introduced the Progressive Interactive Learning Network (PILN), which refines features at global, intermediate, and local levels. Park et al. [17] proposed the dynamic DRSAN, whose structure changes according to input statistics to balance complexity and performance.

Following their success in high-level vision and Natural Language Processing (NLP), Transformers have more recently been adapted to SR tasks. Chen et al. [18] introduced the Pre-trained Image Processing Transformer (IPT) for various low-level visual tasks. Subsequent work has further refined these architectures for complex image restoration problems. The Efficient Attention Pyramid Transformer (EAPT) [19], for instance, was proposed to improve feature representations in general image processing. Meanwhile, Swin Transformer-based dual-branch networks such as SCNet [20] have shown strong capability in recovering structural details. Choi et al. [21] incorporated N-Gram contexts into Transformers and used a sliding-window self-attention mechanism to enlarge the receptive field for degraded-pixel recovery.

Despite these developments, Transformer-based SR methods still have several limitations. In current window-based architectures, self-attention is generally computed within non-overlapping local windows. This constraint limits feature aggregation and often produces blocking artifacts or structural inconsistencies, which can reduce the overall quality of the reconstructed image.

To address these issues, this paper proposes GSDAT-Net, a Grid-Spatial Dual Attention-driven residual hybrid Transformer for image super-resolution. The proposed network effectively fuses multi-scale features to extract rich contextual information. Built on the Swin Transformer architecture, the algorithm incorporates S2TL to strengthen long-range dependency modeling and improve contextual feature aggregation, resulting in richer feature representations. In addition, we design a Fusion Attention Block (FAB) that combines S2TL with ESA. By exploiting both local and non-local priors, the FAB is intended to capture image high-frequency details more efficiently. Based on attention mechanisms and receptive-field optimization, grid attention is further introduced to jointly model similar features across neighborhoods through the hierarchical extraction of channel dimensions, enabling comprehensive cross-neighborhood information interaction.

The main contributions of GSDAT-Net are summarized as follows:

1. We adapt the shifted-window self-attention mechanism of the original STL and design the S2TL module to strengthen contextual representation and expand the effective attention range. This improves the network’s ability to represent complex textures and fine structures.

## 1. Introduction

Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR) is a fundamental task in computer vision that aims to recover high-fidelity details from degraded, low-resolution (LR) observations. Beyond its theoretical value, researchers have investigated SISR as a preprocessing technique for several domain-specific imaging tasks, including medical imaging [1,2], biometric analysis [3,4], and remote sensing [5,6]. The present study, however, focuses exclusively on standard natural-image SR benchmarks and does not directly evaluate these application scenarios. SISR estimates missing high-frequency information with sophisticated algorithms and improves image reconstruction from low-resolution observations.

Super-resolution (SR) is an inherently ill-posed problem because a low-resolution image may correspond to a large number of high-resolution images rather than a single high-resolution image. Existing methods for reconstructing super-resolution images can be grouped into interpolation-based [7], reconstruction-based [8], and learning-based [9] approaches. Learning-based methods primarily use neural networks to reconstruct images with improved quality.

Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based methods have performed strongly in single-image super-resolution by learning complex nonlinear mappings through deep convolutional architectures. Kim et al. [10], for example, designed the Very Deep Super-Resolution (VDSR) model with twenty convolutional layers by cascading small filters within a deep architecture. Tai et al. [11] proposed a Deep Recursive Residual Network (DRRN) that uses recursive structures and residual learning to control the parameter footprint while increasing network depth. Lai et al. [12] developed the Deep Laplacian Pyramid Super-Resolution Network (LapSRN), which uses recurrent layers to share parameters across pyramid levels, reducing parameter redundancy and improving reconstruction quality.

Attention mechanisms have also been widely integrated into SR tasks to focus the model on key regions. Zhang et al. [13] developed the Deep Residual Channel Attention Network (RCAN), which uses long skip connections and channel attention to improve reconstruction accuracy. Xu et al. [14] used Enhanced Densely Connected Attention Residual Groups to construct the EASR network. Yu et al. [15] introduced the reference-based R-DHAN, which employs a texture transfer backbone (SRNTT) to recover rich details at ×4 magnification. Qin et al. [16] proposed the Progressive Interactive Learning Network (PILN), which refines features at global, intermediate, and local levels. Park et al. [17] introduced the dynamic DRSAN, which adjusts its structure according to input statistics to balance complexity and performance.

Following their success in high-level vision and Natural Language Processing (NLP), Transformers have recently been adapted for SR tasks. Chen et al. [18] introduced the Pre-trained Image Processing Transformer (IPT) to handle various low-level visual tasks. Subsequent work has further optimized these architectures for complex image restoration scenarios. The Efficient Attention Pyramid Transformer (EAPT) [19], for instance, was proposed to improve feature representations in general image processing. ### 5. Conclusions

Raw signals from different dense states vary considerably, and a single state may exhibit several representative time–frequency response patterns. At the same time, different states can overlap substantially, especially in dominant peak locations, peak-number configurations, and energy-distribution characteristics. These findings show that relying on a single peak location or a limited number of empirical spectral criteria is inadequate for reliable discrimination during the early stages of micro-void formation.

A multidimensional feature system was established from the raw impact-echo signals, including time-domain statistical features, spectral peak-structure features, sub-band energy features, and normalized energy features. ### 5. Discussion

This work presents GSDAT-Net, an improved single-image super-resolution reconstruction network, and provides a comprehensive evaluation of its reconstruction capability on standard benchmark datasets. Quantitative results across widely used testing scenarios show that the proposed method outperforms recent state-of-the-art SR models, including SwinIR, Omni-SR, and CAMixerSR, in terms of PSNR and SSIM under standard upscaling factors. On the widely adopted Set5, Set14, BSD100, and Urban100 datasets, GSDAT-Net achieves competitive numerical performance, particularly at the ×2 upsampling scale, where it obtains favorable metric values on most test subsets. Its consistent improvements under standard upscaling factors further demonstrate stable and reliable reconstruction performance in objective quantitative evaluations.

These improvements can be attributed to the rational architectural design and efficient feature modeling enabled by the embedded ESA and GAB modules. The proposed S2TL feature extraction unit strengthens the modeling of long-range contextual dependencies, while the cross-neighborhood interaction strategy used in grid attention addresses the inherent feature-aggregation limitations of conventional window-based self-attention. Together, these components allow the network to capture high-frequency edge features and subtle texture details in complex images more accurately. Visual ablation and comparison experiments further confirm the effectiveness of the core modules. Compared with existing CNN-Transformer hybrid algorithms, GSDAT-Net substantially reduces reconstruction artifacts such as edge blurring, texture distortion, and structural dislocation, producing high-fidelity visual results that closely match the real HR reference images.

Despite these advantages, the proposed method has several practical limitations. Under the challenging ×3 and ×4 high-magnification settings, its performance remains slightly limited on certain complex urban scenes in the Urban100 dataset. This limitation is mainly attributable to differences in style across datasets and to the uneven feature-reconstruction preferences of different network paradigms. In addition, compared with ultra-lightweight pure CNN methods, the cascaded dual-module design inevitably introduces greater computational and parameter overhead.

GSDAT-Net also currently learns a deterministic mapping from LR to HR images and therefore does not explicitly model the diversity of plausible HR solutions. Normalizing-flow-based methods, such as SRFlow and HCFlow, provide a probabilistic alternative by learning the conditional distribution of HR images. Moreover, inspired by pixel attention and structured doubly stochastic similarity learning, the introduction of balanced row- and column-wise constraints into grid attention may improve pixel- or patch-level interactions for spatially non-uniform image reconstruction.

Future research will examine probabilistic image restoration approaches, including normalizing-flow-based distribution modeling and doubly stochastic attention constraints. We will also investigate efficient model optimization strategies, such as network pruning, adaptive attention mechanisms, and low-computation feature fusion, with the aim of reducing computational complexity and inference latency while preserving reconstruction performance.

Adults typically select a preferred walking speed that minimizes energy expenditure and maximizes efficiency [6]. With advancing age, both preferred speed and energetic efficiency decline, resulting in a higher metabolic cost during locomotion [7,8]. These increases have been linked to age-related reductions in muscle efficiency, altered gait mechanics, and compensatory control strategies [9]. Yet while the metabolic cost of walking and the mechanical characteristics of gait have each been extensively studied, they are rarely examined together in large samples of older adults. The extant of the literature has predominantly studied gait kinematics or kinetics in isolation, without concurrent measurement of metabolic demands. Conversely, as concluded by a recent report from the National Institute on Aging, there is a limited amount of knowledge that pairs metabolic investigations of walking economy with biomechanical contributors in robust samples [9].As a result, the multidimensional associations between gait characteristics and the metabolic cost of walking remain incompletely understood, particularly in older adults. A small number of studies have attempted to link spatiotemporal parameters with energy expenditure, but most have relied on a small set of variables, low sample sizes and lack of low functioning older adults that preclude generalizable inferences [10]. Moreover, correlations between gait and metabolic metrics have not been studied comprehensively, leaving the overall pattern of associations unexamined. With aging, the decline in both subsystems may produce a mismatch between motor execution and metabolic cost, leading to the characteristic slowing of gait with aging. Mapping the relationship between detailed gait features and metabolic outcomes can help identify which gait characteristics are most consistently associated with walking energetic performance. Identifying gait performance associated with relatively lower or higher metabolic demand may provide useful insight into mobility performance and help guide future investigations.Recent advances in portable and sensor-based assessment have created new opportunities to quantify mobility outside of traditional motion-capture environments. Instrumented walkways such as GaitRite (CIR Systems, Franklin, NJ, USA) provide objective spatiotemporal gait measurements from pressure-sensing technology, while portable indirect calorimetry systems quantify oxygen consumption and energy expenditure during walking. 5. Conclusions

This paper proposed a delay-embedding procedure for indirect sensing in oscillating and periodically forced sensors. The sensor and its excitation are modeled as a single autonomous system: the measurand is treated as a slowly varying state over the reconstruction window, while the excitation is represented by a phase variable. Delayed output samples then define an observation map, whose inverse is approximated by a feedforward neural network.

Compared with the scalar-output conference prequel, the formulation was extended to vector-valued outputs, making it possible to exploit additional channels or known reference signals. The method was applied to a vibratory MEMS gyroscope for signed angular-rate reconstruction. This micromechanical sensor has nonlinear electromechanical transduction, and its raw capacitive current alone does not produce a well-posed problem over a signed domain: opposite angular rates become indistinguishable after a phase shift in the excitation. The problem was resolved by augmenting the output with the known AC drive reference, which provides the missing phase information without requiring an additional mechanical measurement.

The Jacobian-based indicator λmin(J⊤J) served as a local necessary condition. The augmented map was better conditioned than the raw map, and, under ideal conditions, the learned inverse reconstructed the signed angular rate with small errors. A preliminary robustness assessment was also performed. When additive white Gaussian noise was applied to the current channel, the instantaneous per-window estimate was perturbed; however, because the angular rate varies slowly, first-order low-pass post-filtering of the reconstructed sequence reduced the error to the order of magnitude of specialized model-based estimators.

The proposed method is complementary to dedicated model-based estimators. Rather than maximizing accuracy for a single device, it provides a common reconstruction workflow that transfers across heterogeneous oscillating sensors, does not require tuning process- and measurement-noise covariance matrices, and can, in principle, reconstruct additional internal states or physical parameters from the same embedded representation.

Throughout this study, the sensor model was assumed to be accurately known, and robustness to parametric uncertainty was deliberately left outside the scope of the analysis. This choice reflects established practice for vibratory MEMS gyroscopes, where parameter deviations caused by fabrication tolerances, aging, and environmental conditions are a well-known and nontrivial issue. Such deviations are conventionally handled either through dedicated calibration procedures, which identify or compensate for the actual device behavior, or through adaptive and observer-based schemes that estimate the uncertain parameters online. The latter, however, require observability; in the adaptive literature, this requirement takes the form of a persistent-excitation condition enforced through specific control and parameter-update laws [25].

The proposed framework offers a natural route toward the same objective. Because the delay-embedding formulation can accommodate additional slowly varying states, drifting physical parameters could, in principle, be appended to the compact state and estimated jointly with the measurand. Depending on the admissible parameter range, local observability may either hold natively under the present single-frequency interrogation or need to be enforced by enriching the exosystem signal that excites the sensor with additional frequency components, thereby restoring the persistent-excitation requirement of adaptive schemes. As with the measurand itself, this local verification is necessary but not sufficient, since the practical reconstructability of the augmented inverse also depends on the global injectivity of the delay-output map.

Future work could proceed in four directions. First, global injectivity could be investigated more systematically through pairwise-distance or manifold-overlap analyses that complement the local indicator; in the present work, threshold identification and grid-point density still require formal consideration. Second, the effects of sampling time, embedding dimension, excitation frequency, and reference-channel synchronization require further study. Third, noise robustness could be addressed with more advanced estimation schemes, such as a Kalman filter that uses the delayed-output stack as a noisy full-state measurement, or by retraining the inverse map on noisy data to further reduce the residual error and recover the full internal state. ## 2. Hardware and Data Collection

Our work extends the tissue perfusion classification study by Soto et al. [20] by addressing the camera calibration that was previously omitted. This section briefly describes the dataset and the calibration procedure.

### 2.1. TTPD

The Tourniquet Tissue Perfusion Dataset (TTPD) was collected at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, using a prototype multimodal data acquisition device. For each volunteer, relevant images were obtained using three different methods. The system included a thermal infrared camera (FLIR A700, Teledyne FLIR, Wilsonville, OR, USA; 640 × 480 resolution), an RGB camera (Arducam, Nanjing, China; 1200 × 1200 resolution), and a Laser Speckle Contrast Imaging (LSCI) modality based on a customized Arducam camera with its IR filter removed (2000 × 2000 resolution). A software-based trigger system provided temporal synchronization across the three modalities, allowing frames to be captured simultaneously with a minimal millisecond delay tolerance. This tolerance is more than sufficient given the recording rate of 1 frame per second (fps).

Images were collected every second while the participants experienced arterial and venous blockage produced by a tourniquet, simulating different tissue perfusion conditions. The initial 60 s pre-pressure phase (0pre) was used to obtain baseline measurements. The following 120 s phase produced arterial blockage (1tq1), and the subsequent 60 s phase resulted in venous occlusion (2tq2).

Data were collected from 10 college-aged volunteers, with a mean age of 21 years, and were divided into two experimental scenarios. For Pass2, training used data from all 10 individuals, while testing used data from three individuals who were imaged a second time. Thus, Pass2 evaluates session-based generalization, in which the same subjects are recorded during a separate session. For the Unseen set, training used data from seven individuals, and testing used data from the three remaining participants, representing strict subject-based generalization. Table 1 provides the exact distribution of frames used across all splits.

Examples of the uncalibrated and calibrated data are shown in Figures 1 and 2, respectively. This pilot dataset consisted primarily of fair-skinned individuals, and only three of the ten participants were female.

### 2.2. Calibration

Prior work used resized images directly for classification and reported promising results. However, resizing the laser and RGB images to match the lower-resolution thermal images distorted their aspect ratios. In addition, early fusion without calibration produces image stacks that are not spatially aligned, which may reduce the feature extraction capability of a CNN. Here, we investigate whether appropriate calibration can improve performance.

A standard checkerboard calibration procedure was used to image the experimental volume, shown at the bottom of Figure 2. Although the laser and RGB cameras produced crisp images, the thermal images were of poor quality. To make the checkerboard visible in the thermal images, the pattern was placed in the sun so that the black squares would heat more than the white squares. However, the heat dissipated quickly, producing blurry edges and corners. As a result, full multi-camera 3D calibration was not possible. Stereo calibration between the laser and RGB cameras would have been feasible, but stereo calibration involving the thermal images was not possible because the corners could not be located reliably.

Instead, a homography-based calibration method [21] was used to align the ground plane of the experimental volume. For each modality, the four corresponding checkerboard corner points were selected manually and used to compute a transformation matrix relative to a standardized rectangular grid. Although a formal point-perturbation stability analysis was not performed, careful manual visual verification and the subsequent improvements in downstream classification accuracy empirically support the robustness of the estimated matrices. The Four Point Algorithm uses the checkerboard corner points, shown as red dots at the bottom of Figure 2, to generate a homography transformation that warps all images into a common ground-plane view.

After the homography warp, the images were adjusted using bicubic interpolation. Because the transformation aligns the modalities with a physically uniform checkerboard grid, it inherently corrects aspect ratio distortion. Boundary areas outside the valid image region after the perspective warp were uniformly zero-padded. Since CNNs use spatial translation invariance, these zero-padded regions provide a consistent static background across all calibrated images and prevent the regions from being learned as artificial discriminative features.

Figure 1 presents example images and overlays without calibration. The images show a clear offset when overlaid. In particular, the LSCI+RGB example contains two O2 monitors, and the hand exhibits an offset of approximately 60 pixels. Figure 2 shows the same images after the homography transformation, with strong alignment between the hands across the different modalities. This alignment is expected to provide better features for classification. Because of the homography transformation, warped images may contain blank areas, such as the black regions at the top, and may exhibit only partial overlap along the edges. In addition, the homography transformation assumes a flat ground plane, so objects above the ground plane, including the thickness of the hand, will exhibit some distortion.

ConclusionsThis paper focuses on the study of the error sources, modeling methods and compensation strategies of weighing rain gauges in complex environments, focusing on the analysis of the formation mechanism of five major error factors, namely, creep error, vibration interference, temperature drift, residual error and random error, and using experimental data to construct an environmentally adaptable error mathematical model. However, typical operating areas, such as discharge zones, often contain many large obstacles, including multiple mining trucks parked in parallel or in an interleaved arrangement, fluctuating earth and rock piles, large-area slopes, and retaining walls. Nevertheless, LiDAR depends on the linear emission and reflection of infrared beams and therefore cannot penetrate solid obstacles. Under complex occlusion, extensive blind spots can appear within the LiDAR scanning field. In particular, close-range occlusions can cause a single-LiDAR system to completely miss hidden targets. This missing data prevents the planning and control modules from recognizing hidden risks and may result in collisions.

In recent years, 4D millimeter-wave radar has attracted attention because its longer electromagnetic wavelength provides greater potential for non-line-of-sight (NLOS) detection through multipath diffraction and penetration. This capability creates a new means of detecting hidden obstacles behind foreground occlusions. However, in mining environments, electromagnetic waves undergo severe multipath reflections between large metallic truck chassis and the unstructured ground. As a result, radar point clouds contain substantial multipath ghost targets beneath the surface, which severely interfere with accurate target extraction. At the same time, most existing perception studies remain focused on urban environments and use datasets such as KITTI and nuScenes, which are difficult to transfer directly to the harsh physical conditions of open-pit mines. Although specialized mining datasets such as AutoMine have recently emerged, they primarily address LOS perception and lack multimodal data designed for NLOS conditions in open-pit mines.

Blind-spot completion and occlusion-reasoning mechanisms for hidden obstacles remain insufficiently studied. Existing deep-learning-based Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) and late-fusion strategies generally assume, often implicitly, that each modality can effectively observe the targets. In extreme mining scenarios, one sensor may experience severe physical occlusion while another provides only sparse signals. Under these conditions, pure feature interaction without physical spatial guidance tends to be unstable. Table 1 summarizes the limitations of existing methods and identifies the research gap addressed in this study.

Its purpose is to use calibrated LiDAR–radar point clouds and physical blind-zone constraints to complement LiDAR perception under asymmetric visibility, particularly when complete annotated datasets for open-pit NLOS scenarios are unavailable.

## 2. Method

HD-sEMG signals contain rich information in the temporal, frequency, and spatial domains. STDC-Net incorporates features from all three domains to improve the understanding of how much attention the network gives to each type of feature. The overall architecture of STDC-Net is shown in Figure 1.

The Feature Channel focuses on temporal- and frequency-domain features extracted from HD-sEMG signals, thereby facilitating rapid network convergence. SHAP values are used to rank feature contributions, with larger values indicating higher priority, or greater importance for classification. The Spatial Channel focuses on temporal- and spatial-domain features by combining temporal convolutional layers with spatial graph attention layers. Its input is the original HD-sEMG signal. Temporal features are extracted using 1D convolutional layers followed by the gated linear unit (GLU) [31], which introduces nonlinearity and compensates for incomplete information in the Feature Channel. The graph attention layers then capture spatial-domain features, followed by channel connection maps that illustrate the synergy between muscles.

### 2.1. Feature Channel with Convolutional Layers

To examine the extent to which the network attends to different features during gesture recognition, widely used EMG classification features are extracted and ranked, including 15 time-domain features and 6 frequency-domain features. Incorporating all features previously applied in similar tasks [32,33,34] provides a clearer understanding of which features contribute most to classification performance.

The 2D convolutional layers process information across the feature and channel dimensions to obtain high-dimensional feature representations. Locally connected layers then refine the detailed feature extraction. Because convolution weights at different spatial positions are not shared, the network can learn multi-scale features and improve its ability to recognize specific local patterns. The detailed structure of the Feature Channel is shown in Figure 2.

The Feature Channel receives a 2D input of size 21 (handcrafted features) × 128 (EMG channels). It contains two standard 2D convolutional blocks with 3 × 3 kernels and 16 → 64 filters, followed by batch normalization, ReLU, and max-pooling. These are followed by two locally connected blocks with 64 filters and a dropout rate of 0.5 to capture position-specific patterns. A final fully connected layer compresses the feature map into a 64-dimensional embedding.

The 15 time-domain features are waveform length (WL), slope sign change (SSC), root mean square (RMS), kurtosis (KU), Willison amplitude (WAMP), zero crossing (ZC), median, mean, max, min, peak to peak (PK), average rectified value (ARV), variance (VA), standard deviation (ST), and skewness (SK). The 6 frequency-domain features are total power, mean frequency (Mean_freq), median frequency (Median_freq), peak frequency (Peak_freq), average power (Avg_power), and spectral entropy value (Entropy_val).

After classification, SHAP values are used to assess the contribution of each feature. SHAP is a widely used feature-attribution method in explainable AI. It is derived from cooperative game theory (CGT) and is used to explain prediction results, particularly for black-box models [35]. SHAP quantifies the contribution of each feature by expressing the model prediction as the sum of the Shapley values of the input features.

### 2.2. Spatial Channel with Graph Attention Layers

The Spatial Channel consists of temporal convolutional layers and spatial graph attention layers, as shown in Figure 3. The temporal convolutional layers are constructed using 1D convolutional layers and GLUs. They automatically extract features and supplement information that may be omitted by the Feature Channel. Although CNNs are effective for processing grid-like inputs in Euclidean space, they may have difficulty handling non-Euclidean structures such as HD-sEMG signals. Graph attention layers are therefore used to model the topological relationships within the HD-sEMG signals.

The Spatial Channel processes raw HD-sEMG signals with 128 channels and 100 time samples. Temporal features are extracted through three 1D convolutional blocks with a kernel size of 3, 128 filters, and pool sizes of 2, 2, and 5, reducing the temporal dimension to 5. A k-nearest neighbor graph with k = 2 is dynamically constructed from the resulting 128 node features, each with a dimension of 5. Two single-head GAT layers, with dimensions 5 → 64 and 64 → 64, perform spatial message passing. Global mean pooling and a fully connected layer then produce a 64-dimensional embedding. The GAT outputs attention weights that are used to generate channel connection maps.

The graph attention layer introduces an attention mechanism into a graph neural network operating in the spatial domain. It updates node features through the representations of neighboring nodes rather than through complex computations such as Laplace matrices. During feature aggregation, the attention mechanism determines the weights of neighboring nodes [36]. To make the coefficients comparable across nodes, the attention coefficients are generally expressed as Equation (1):

\[
\alpha_{ij}=\operatorname{Softmax}(e_{ij})
=\frac{\exp\left(\alpha W H_i^{k-1}, W H_j^{k-1}\right)}
{\sum_{l\in N_i}\exp\left(\alpha W H_i^{k-1}, W H_l^{k-1}\right)}
\tag{1}
\]

where \(e_{ij}\) represents the strength of the relationship between node \(i\) and node \(j\); \(W\) denotes the weight matrix; and \(H^{k-1}\) represents the hidden node features in the \((k-1)\)th layer. Each node attends only to its neighboring nodes, and \(\alpha_{ij}\) is interpreted as the transfer probability from node \(i\) to each neighboring node.

Channel connection maps are generated from the outputs of the graph attention layer and reflect the connection weights between channels. These maps provide a better understanding of muscle interactions.

ConclusionsAimed at performance and robustness optimization of electronically controlled fuel injectors in a high-pressure fuel system, the following optimization design process was proposed. First, the sensitivity and interaction of key control parameters are analyzed, and the sensitivity ranking of key control parameters on performance indexes such as circulating fuel injection quantity, fuel injection duration, fuel flow rate and air/fuel ratio under known disturbance is given; At the same time, robustness optimization and tolerance analysis are carried out according to each design variable. Then, taking the target quantities for circulating fuel injection quantity as the optimization objective, a basic parameter design scheme with good robustness is obtained by the optimization and calculation of key control parameters. ### 3. FEBio Simulation

The problem was treated as static structural mechanics. Figure 1 presents the simulation, and Table 2 describes its elements. The applied indentation ranged from 0 to 20 mm.

The shear-wave speed in undeformed tissue is defined as the tissue’s base speed, \(c_{s0}\). For every indentation step, the principal stretches of each tissue element within the ultrasound field of view were recorded. At each indentation, these principal stretches produced a proportional increase in the tissue’s base speed. The proportional increase, \(P\), relative to the base speed \(c_{s0}\), was calculated for stiffening parameters in the ranges \(0.01 < \alpha < 100\) and \(0.01 < C_2 < 100\), as shown in Equations (7)–(9). The proportional-increase field represents the increase from the base-speed value within the area of interest and does not depend on the base parameter.

Figure 2 illustrates the deformation pattern produced by the probe in polar coordinates.

The greatest change in \(\lambda\) occurred at the point of contact between the probe and the tissue. The effect extended outward from the contact point, decreasing in magnitude with increasing distance from the probe. The area of effect at different threshold intensities, \(AOE_{\text{thres}}\), was defined as the number of pixels in which the proportional increase from the base speed exceeded the threshold.

The magnitude of the change increased with indentation. Figure 3 shows the differences in areas at various thresholds as the indentation level increased. The thresholds ranged from a proportional increase of 1.10 to 3.00 relative to the base speed.

## 1. Introduction

Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) provide an important benchmark for the Internet of Things (IoT), using recent technologies to optimize communication and safety systems in hazardous environments [1,2,3]. Because they enable real-time data collection at low cost, WSNs are becoming increasingly popular in various application areas, including tele-surgery, intelligent transportation, smart homes, industrial control, the business sector, virtual reality, and law enforcement [4,5,6]. WSNs must be highly flexible, scalable, interoperable, and reliable. They must also address several challenges, such as improving energy efficiency, supporting environmental monitoring, and enhancing social services [2]. Low power consumption is a primary requirement for the continued deployment of independent battery-powered devices and for reducing maintenance costs, since most nodes are installed in unattended locations.

Cost-effectiveness and energy efficiency will remain significant research challenges in the coming years. In addition, the increasing complexity of applications is creating a technological gap with the limited amount of energy available in sensor nodes. Because sensor nodes have limited computing capabilities, their workload is often restricted to simple calculations. Energy savings can therefore be achieved by using a processing unit with variable-speed processors [7,8,9]. Changing either the frequency or the voltage inevitably reduces energy consumption [8]. This is the basis of the DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling) technique, which manages the voltage-frequency pair while maintaining a sufficiently high level of performance. The DPM (Dynamic Power Management) technique controls the standby and active states of a node. Efficient management of these power modes contributes to saving energy resources [10].

This paper describes how combining different techniques within scheduling algorithms can advance current research on WSNs and draw attention to aspects of these algorithms that are sometimes overlooked. However, applying DVFS and DPM mechanisms to reduce dissipated power can cause job deadlines to be missed. To address this issue, the developed Hybrid Energy-Efficient Power manager Scheduling (HEEPS) integrates a hybrid approach that combines several multi-objective techniques. It uses task migration, DPM time-out2, in which a task that remains idle for a given duration switches to the “DeepSleep” state, and intertask DVFS, in which the speed of each task is fixed and cannot be changed between its different instances. A global scheduling strategy based on Earliest Deadline First (EDF), known for its robustness, is then applied. In addition, we introduce original modifications by combining the conditions of Goossens, Funk, and Baruah (GFB) [11] with those of Srinivasan and Belkadi (SB) [12]. In this context, the authors of [13] proposed the HEEPS concept and its model for use in wireless communications and WSNs.

This paper presents the current stage of an activity developed over several years, with particular attention given to the following contributions:

- A novel WSN energy-saving model, called HEEPS, is developed to schedule real-time tasks by combining power management and scheduling techniques. HEEPS provides a customized energy-management algorithm based on DPM time-out 2 and intertask DVFS, driven by the GEDF (Generalised Earliest Deadline First) scheduler to meet application requirements. The implemented power model uses power states as a methodology for modeling power consumption.
- A comprehensive review of various energy-saving techniques for WSNs is provided. Each technique aims to improve the efficiency of a sensor node, including energy harvesting and clock gating. A discussion demonstrating the efficiency of the proposed algorithm and comparing it with similar methods in the literature is also presented.
- Time constraints are specified and verified through the GEDF scheduler by combining two scheduling conditions to avoid the Dhall effect and non-exploited resources:
  (a) the condition of Goossens, Funk, and Baruah;
  (b) the condition of Srinivasan and Belkadi.
- The influences of the number of tasks, number of CPUs, Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET), Average Execution Time (AET), workload, and other factors on energy savings achieved by HEEPS are evaluated using the STORM simulator. Detailed performance analyses and experimental results are provided, showing greater energy savings than those achieved by other existing methods.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents an in-depth investigation of energy-minimization techniques and compares their performance. Section 3 describes the HEEPS energy-management model. Section 4 presents the configuration used in the simulation experiments. The results and evaluation metrics are discussed in Section 5. Section 6 examines the relevance of the proposed approach in relation to existing work. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper.
